transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the main thing is… I’ve been having this problem where I’m not really taking in what people are saying, even when I’m trying to listen. The example that finally made me think I should come in is with my wife. She’ll be telling me something practical, like about my cousin’s appointments or who needs a ride where, and I’ll be sitting there looking right at her, nodding along, and then maybe a minute later I realize I only caught bits and pieces of it.

It’s not like I’m trying to ignore her. I really am looking at her, and I think I’m listening, but then it’s like the words didn’t fully land. And then I feel embarrassed because she thinks I wasn’t paying attention, and honestly, I can’t really argue with that because I don’t remember half of what she just said. That’s the sort of thing that brought me in.
Do you feel like you’re actually hearing the words clearly when people speak, but they still don’t register?

Yes, that’s exactly how it feels. I mean, I can hear her fine — it’s not like she’s mumbling or like the room is too loud necessarily. She’ll be talking to me about something pretty straightforward, like my cousin’s appointments or who needs a ride and when, and I’m sitting there looking right at her, nodding like I’m following.

But then a minute later, it’s like I realize only part of it actually stuck. I’ll remember maybe the general topic, but not the details she just told me. And that’s the frustrating part, because in the moment I would swear I was listening. It just doesn’t seem to fully register.
Does this mainly happen when people are speaking to you, rather than when you read the same information yourself?

Yeah, I think so — at least that’s the main way I’m noticing it. It’s really when someone is talking to me, especially my wife, and it’s something practical like my cousin’s appointments or rides or what time somebody needs to be somewhere. I’ll be looking right at her, and I’m not off doing something else, so from the outside it probably looks like I’m taking it in.

But then, honestly, a minute later I’ll realize I didn’t really absorb half of what she said. I might remember, “Okay, this was about an appointment,” but not the actual time or who was supposed to do what. That’s the part that made me feel like I should probably talk to someone about it, because it keeps happening even when I think I’m listening.
When someone is speaking, do you ever feel like you hear the sounds clearly but still have trouble making sense of the words themselves?

I don’t know if I’d say I can’t make sense of the words exactly. It’s more like… I hear her talking clearly, and I know she’s speaking English and I’m following the general idea at first, but it just doesn’t settle in.

Like with my wife, she’ll be telling me about my cousin’s appointments or who needs a ride, and I’ll be looking right at her, nodding along, and I really do think I’m listening. But then a minute later I’ll realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said — the time, or who was supposed to go where, or whatever the important detail was.

So it’s not that the words sound garbled. It’s more that they pass through without me really holding onto them, if that makes sense.
When this happens, do you notice that your mind has drifted to something else while the person is talking?

Yes, I think that is what’s happening a lot of the time. I don’t always catch it right away, but if I really think about it, I’ll start off listening fine and then somewhere in the middle my mind just sort of wanders off.

It happens in other situations too, not just with my wife. Like if I sit down to work out a catering order, I can begin pretty organized — looking at the quantities, who asked for what, what needs to be written down — and then after a bit I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the same part and my mind was somewhere else entirely. Then I have to go back over the notes like I never read them in the first place.

Same thing if I’m listening through a parish planning call. I’ll mean to follow it, and at the beginning I usually do, but after a while I’ll notice I’ve missed a chunk of what was said. It’s not dramatic, exactly, but it’s frustrating because I’m not trying to tune out. It’s like my attention just doesn’t stay where I put it.
Thinking back to when you were a child in school, did you already have this kind of trouble staying focused and taking in what people were saying?

Yes, I think so. I mean, going back that far is a little fuzzy in some ways, but that part actually does stand out because it was something my parents heard from teachers more than once.

In grade school, definitely before I was 12, the message was usually something like, “He’s bright, but he’s always daydreaming,” or “He can do the work, but he doesn’t finish unless someone reminds him.” I remember teachers saying I’d leave homework in my desk, or I’d have done part of something and then just not turn it in, or I’d need reminders to get back to the classwork when everyone else was already moving along.

At the time I don’t think anyone framed it as a serious problem. It was more like I was spacey or not applying myself, which was frustrating because I wasn’t trying to ignore people. But yes, when I think about what’s happening now with conversations not really sinking in, there was probably a version of that even back then.
Does this kind of losing focus create problems for you in more than one part of your life, like at work, at home, or in other responsibilities?

Yes, it does. I mean, I wouldn’t say my whole life is falling apart from it, but it’s showing up in more than one place.

At home it’s probably the most uncomfortable, because with my cousin’s care there are appointments, rides, little details that actually matter, and my wife will tell me something and then later I’ll have to ask again or I’ll have missed part of it. And I can tell she gets frustrated — not just annoyed, more like she feels she can’t really count on me to hold onto the information. That creates tension between us, because I don’t want her feeling like she has to carry everything or check behind me all the time.

And then with catering-type tasks, even small ones, I’ve had to go back and double-check or redo things because I’m worried I mixed up a detail or didn’t really absorb what was written down. It’s not usually some huge disaster, but it slows me down and makes simple jobs take longer than they should. I’ll think, “Wait, did I put the right quantity here?” or “Was that for this order or the other one?” and then I have to retrace it so I don’t mess it up.

So yes, it’s home responsibilities and work-type responsibilities both. It’s mild in the sense that I can usually catch it if I double-check, but the fact that I have to keep doing that is the problem.
When you’re doing something that really interests you, is it still hard to keep your attention on it?

Yes, even then, though it’s probably a little better if I’m genuinely interested. It’s not like I can’t pay attention at all. I can start off fine, and sometimes I’m really trying to stay with it.

But if I sit down to work out a catering order, for example, even if I care about getting it right, I’ll begin with the quantities and the notes and think, “Okay, I’ve got this.” Then before long I realize I’ve drifted. I might be staring at the same line or the same part of the order, and I don’t really remember taking it in. So I have to go back over the notes like I never read them in the first place.

Same sort of thing with a parish planning call. I may want to follow what’s being said, especially if it involves something I care about, but after a while my mind wanders and I miss pieces of it. Then I’m trying to catch up or figure out what was just decided. So interest helps some, but it doesn’t completely keep my attention locked in.
As a child, were you often fidgety or unable to stay seated when you were expected to?

I’m not really sure, honestly. That part doesn’t stand out to me the same way the daydreaming and not finishing things does.

I don’t remember being the kid who was constantly out of his seat or running around the classroom when I wasn’t supposed to. I mean, I was a child, so I’m sure I moved around some, and maybe I tapped a pencil or shifted in my chair like kids do, but I don’t have a clear memory of teachers complaining that I couldn’t sit still.

If anything, the feedback I remember was more that I seemed somewhere else mentally, not that I was physically all over the place. But I’m also relying on old memories, so I don’t want to say it never happened — I just don’t really have that as part of the picture in my mind.
Has this problem with your attention been fairly consistent throughout your adult life?

I’d say it’s been noticeably harder for about the last 11 months. That’s really when it started standing out to me more — since my cousin moved in with us after surgery.

I may have had little moments before where I’d lose track of things or have to reread something, but the part that feels like a real problem, the part where it’s affecting responsibilities and making me feel like I’m dropping pieces of information, that’s been mostly this past year. Once my cousin was living with us, there were just more things to keep straight, and I started seeing how often my attention would slip.

So no, I don’t think I’d describe it as equally consistent all through my adult life. It’s been more obvious and harder to manage these last 11 months.
Over these last 11 months, have you been feeling persistently worried or on edge most days?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I’ve had things on my mind, sure, and there are days where I feel strained or preoccupied, but I don’t know that I’ve been persistently worried or on edge most days in the way you’re asking.

It’s more like I notice the attention problems and then I get bothered by the consequences of that, if that makes sense. But I haven’t really thought of myself as walking around anxious all the time or constantly keyed up. Maybe I’d need you to clarify what you mean by “on edge,” because I could be missing it, but it hasn’t stood out to me as the main thing.
Over these last 11 months, have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I’ve had frustrating days, definitely, and there are times when I get discouraged about not keeping up with things the way I think I should. But when you say “down or depressed most days,” that sounds more constant than what I’ve noticed.

I wouldn’t describe the last 11 months as me feeling depressed day after day. More like... I get annoyed with myself, or I feel a little worn out by trying to stay on top of things, but I don’t wake up most mornings feeling like everything is hopeless or that I’m in a dark mood all the time.

So I guess my answer is no, not most days. At least not in the way I understand depression. If there’s a specific kind of feeling you mean, I can try to think about it that way.
Do you feel this got noticeably worse after your cousin moved in and the added responsibilities started?

Yes, that’s when it became noticeable to me. I don’t want to make it sound like there was one exact day where everything changed, but after my cousin moved in with us after the surgery, the added responsibilities made it harder to keep track of things.

It’s been about 11 months now, and that’s really the stretch of time where I started thinking, okay, this is becoming more of a problem than just being absentminded here and there. Before that, I may have had little lapses, but it didn’t stand out in the same way. Since then, with more to manage, it’s felt noticeably harder.
Since your cousin moved in, have you felt overwhelmed by the added responsibilities?

Yes, I have. I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart or anything, but it has felt like more than I can smoothly keep in my head.

The biggest place it shows up is at home. My wife gets frustrated because with my cousin’s care, she feels like she can’t fully count on me to remember or follow through the way she needs me to. And I understand why she feels that way, which makes it worse, because I’m not trying to be careless. It’s just that there are more moving pieces now, and if I don’t write things down or check back, something can slip.

And then with the catering stuff I still help with, even the smaller jobs have started taking more effort because I’ll double-check myself or have to redo parts so things don’t get mixed up. It’s not huge disasters, but it’s enough that it creates extra work and tension. So, yes, “overwhelmed” is probably fair, especially when the responsibilities pile up at the same time.
When your attention slips, is it usually because thoughts about your cousin or the added responsibilities suddenly take over your mind?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, sometimes I’m aware there’s more on my plate, and I can feel sort of pressured by all of it, but it doesn’t usually feel like thoughts about my cousin suddenly rush in and take over my whole mind.

It’s more like my attention just kind of drifts or I lose the thread of what I was doing. Then afterward I may realize, oh, I was supposed to remember this other thing too, or I got pulled off track because there are a lot of things to keep straight. But I can’t say I’ve noticed a clear pattern where I’m sitting there doing something and then thoughts about my cousin specifically interrupt me.

So... I don’t know. The added responsibilities are part of the background, definitely, but I haven’t really noticed my mind being hijacked by them in that sudden way you’re asking about.
If your cousin had not moved in with you, do you think these attention problems would still be bothering you this much?

I think… probably not this much. I mean, I can’t say for sure how I’d be if things had stayed the same, because you don’t really get to run both versions of life side by side, but the timing does seem pretty clear to me.

It’s been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since my cousin moved in with us after the surgery. That’s when I started feeling like I was having more trouble keeping up with things and noticing the lapses more. Before that, I might have had some moments here and there, but they didn’t bother me in the same way or stand out as much.

So my best answer is that without my cousin moving in and all of that becoming part of the household, maybe I’d still have occasional issues, but I don’t think they’d be bothering me to this degree.
Did these attention problems become noticeably worse only after your cousin moved in with you?

Yes, that’s how it seems to me. It became noticeably harder after my cousin moved in with us after the surgery.

I’d put it at about 11 months now. Before that, I don’t want to say I was perfect or anything, but it wasn’t standing out to me in the same way. Since he’s been in the house and that whole situation became part of daily life, that’s when I really started noticing it as a problem.
Do you think your attention would go back closer to normal if your cousin were no longer living with you?

I think it might, yes… at least closer to how things were before. I don’t want to say everything would instantly go back to normal, because I don’t really know that, but the change has been noticeable for about 11 months now, since my cousin moved in with us after the surgery.

That’s the point where things started feeling harder for me attention-wise. So if that situation weren’t part of the household anymore, I’d expect maybe the pressure would ease up and my attention might settle back somewhat. I can’t guarantee it, but based on the timing, that’s what I’d guess.
Do you think the extra stress of your cousin living with you is the main reason your attention has been worse?

I think it’s a big part of it, yes. I don’t know if I’d call it the only reason, because that feels a little too definite, but the timing lines up pretty strongly in my mind.

This has been noticeably harder for about 11 months, basically since my cousin moved in with us after the surgery. Before that, it wasn’t like I was thinking about my attention all the time or feeling like it was getting in my way so much. Then once he was in the house and that whole situation became part of everyday life, that’s when I started noticing it more.

So… yes, I’d say the extra stress around that is probably the main thing I connect it to, at least from what I can tell.
When your cousin is away and things are less stressful at home, do you still have the same trouble paying attention?

Yes, I think I do still have some trouble, even when things are quieter. It may not feel as stirred up or as pressured, but it doesn’t completely disappear.

Like, if I sit down to work out a catering order, I can start off okay — I’ll have the list in front of me, the numbers, what needs to be done — but after a little while I realize my mind has gone somewhere else. Then I’m looking back at the same notes thinking, “Did I already read this? Did I count that correctly?” And I have to go back over it again like it didn’t really sink in the first time.

Same kind of thing with a parish planning call. I’ll be listening at the beginning, and I really intend to follow along, but before long I drift. Then someone refers to something that was just said, and I’m trying to piece it together from my notes or memory. So… yes, even when my cousin is away and the house is calmer, I still notice that happening. It’s just maybe not as intense as when everything at home feels stressful.

In grade school, definitely before I was 12, the message was usually something like, “He’s bright, but he’s always daydreaming,” or “He can do the work, but he doesn’t finish unless someone reminds him.” I remember teachers saying I’d leave homework in my desk, or I’d have done part of something and then just not turn it in, or I’d need reminders to get back to the classwork when everyone else was already moving along.

At the time I don’t think anyone framed it as a serious problem. It was more like I was spacey or not applying myself, which was frustrating because I wasn’t trying to ignore people. But yes, when I think about what’s happening now with conversations not really sinking in, there was probably a version of that even back then.

Yes, it does. I mean, I wouldn’t say my whole life is falling apart from it, but it’s showing up in more than one place.

At home it’s probably the most uncomfortable, because with my cousin’s care there are appointments, rides, little details that actually matter, and my wife will tell me something and then later I’ll have to ask again or I’ll have missed part of it. And I can tell she gets frustrated — not just annoyed, more like she feels she can’t really count on me to hold onto the information. That creates tension between us, because I don’t want her feeling like she has to carry everything or check behind me all the time.

And then with catering-type tasks, even small ones, I’ve had to go back and double-check or redo things because I’m worried I mixed up a detail or didn’t really absorb what was written down. It’s not usually some huge disaster, but it slows me down and makes simple jobs take longer than they should. I’ll think, “Wait, did I put the right quantity here?” or “Was that for this order or the other one?” and then I have to retrace it so I don’t mess it up.

So yes, it’s home responsibilities and work-type responsibilities both. It’s mild in the sense that I can usually catch it if I double-check, but the fact that I have to keep doing that is the problem.

Yes, even then, though it’s probably a little better if I’m genuinely interested. It’s not like I can’t pay attention at all. I can start off fine, and sometimes I’m really trying to stay with it.

But if I sit down to work out a catering order, for example, even if I care about getting it right, I’ll begin with the quantities and the notes and think, “Okay, I’ve got this.” Then before long I realize I’ve drifted. I might be staring at the same line or the same part of the order, and I don’t really remember taking it in. So I have to go back over the notes like I never read them in the first place.

Same sort of thing with a parish planning call. I may want to follow what’s being said, especially if it involves something I care about, but after a while my mind wanders and I miss pieces of it. Then I’m trying to catch up or figure out what was just decided. So interest helps some, but it doesn’t completely keep my attention locked in.

I’m not really sure, honestly. That part doesn’t stand out to me the same way the daydreaming and not finishing things does.

I don’t remember being the kid who was constantly out of his seat or running around the classroom when I wasn’t supposed to. I mean, I was a child, so I’m sure I moved around some, and maybe I tapped a pencil or shifted in my chair like kids do, but I don’t have a clear memory of teachers complaining that I couldn’t sit still.

If anything, the feedback I remember was more that I seemed somewhere else mentally, not that I was physically all over the place. But I’m also relying on old memories, so I don’t want to say it never happened — I just don’t really have that as part of the picture in my mind.

I wouldn’t describe the last 11 months as me feeling depressed day after day. More like... I get annoyed with myself, or I feel a little worn out by trying to stay on top of things, but I don’t wake up most mornings feeling like everything is hopeless or that I’m in a dark mood all the time.
